blocks.text: The Raspberry Pi 2 Model B is the second-generation Raspberry Pi single-board computer, designed to provide significantly improved processing performance while maintaining compatibility with the Raspberry Pi ecosystem.

The original Raspberry Pi 2 Model B was introduced with a 900MHz quad-core ARM Cortex-A7 processor and 1GB of LPDDR2 RAM, providing a substantial performance improvement over the previous Raspberry Pi generation. Later revisions of the Raspberry Pi 2 Model B use the BCM2837/B0 processor with a quad-core 64-bit ARM Cortex-A53 CPU.

The board provides a 40-pin GPIO header for connecting sensors, displays, motors, relays, and other electronic modules. It also includes four USB 2.0 ports, 100Mbps Ethernet, a full-size HDMI port, a microSD card slot, and dedicated CSI camera and DSI display interfaces.

With its compact form factor and extensive connectivity, the Raspberry Pi 2 Model B is suitable for a wide range of applications including embedded computing, robotics, automation, education, media projects, networked devices, and prototyping.

Upgraded Camera Sensor: GC2145 vs OV2640
This ESP32-S3 camera module integrates the latest GC2145 (GalaxyCore) 2-MP CMOS sensor, offering a significant upgrade over the legacy OV2640 used in earlier ESP32-CAM modules.

Both sensors provide 2-megapixel resolution, but GC2145 features a larger pixel size (1.75 µm) and a newer generation imaging architecture, resulting in improved low-light performance, reduced noise, and more accurate color reproduction. The sensor supports higher frame rates and smoother video capture, achieving up to 60 fps at optimized resolutions and significantly better motion performance compared to the OV2640 (typically up to 15 fps at full resolution).

What does "3-in-1" mean for the DST-210?
It means one handheld device switches between three functions — oscilloscope, digital multimeter, and DDS signal generator — using a rotary dial, instead of needing three separate instruments.
What's the difference between the DST-210 and the DST-201?
Both share the same multimeter and signal generator functions. The DST-210 has a faster oscilloscope: 48 MSa/s sampling and 10MHz analog bandwidth, versus the DST-201's 5 MSa/s and 1MHz bandwidth.
Can this replace a full bench oscilloscope?
For everyday troubleshooting and field diagnostics, yes. For 2-channel capture, higher bandwidth, or heavier lab work, a dedicated bench oscilloscope like the RIGOL DS1102Z-E is a better fit.
Does it need external probes to work?
Yes — the oscilloscope and signal generator connect via BNC probes (included), and the multimeter uses standard test leads (also included).

name: NX8048P070-011C HMI LCD 7"
desc: Nextion Display Capacitive Touch Screen UART 800 x 480 Human Machine Interface LCD

blocks.text: The NX8048P070-011C Nextion display is a 7 inch HMI touch screen that handles the graphics and touch on its own, so your controller only needs to send and receive short serial messages. As a 7 inch Nextion HMI display with 800x480 resolution and a capacitive touch panel, it suits control panels, smart-home screens, machine interfaces and engineering graduation projects.
NX8048P070-011C – 7.0" Intelligent Series HMI Capacitive Touch Display (No Enclosure)
GPIO: 8 (IO0–IO7); IO6 and IO7 support PWM
SD card: microSD up to 32 GB (FAT32)
GUI elements: Text, number, button, progress bar, image, slider, gauge, QR code, video, audio, switch, combo box, and more
Component features: Transparency, page load effects, animation
Encodings: ASCII, UTF-8, GB2312, Big5, Shift-JIS, and others
7 Inch Nextion HMI Display With 800x480 Capacitive Touch

This 7 inch Nextion HMI display gives you an 800x480 screen (also configurable as 480x800) with 65K colors and a brightness of 300 nit that you can adjust from 0% to 100%. The capacitive touch panel responds to a light touch, which feels closer to a phone screen than a resistive panel. It belongs to the Nextion Intelligent Series, so screens are designed visually instead of being coded pixel by pixel.
Capacitive Touch HMI LCD for UART Control

As a capacitive touch HMI LCD, the NX8048P070-011C keeps the interface work inside the display. You build pages with buttons, sliders, gauges, text and images in the Nextion Editor using drag-and-drop components, then load the project onto the screen. After that, your controller talks to the display over a UART serial connection, sending short commands to change values and receiving touch events back. The serial speed ranges from 2400 to 921600 bps, and the same display works with any controller that has a serial port, such as an Arduino or an ESP32 board.
Nextion UART Display 800x480: Power, GPIO and Storage

This Nextion UART display 800x480 module runs from a 5V supply (operating range 4.75V to 6.5V), and a 5V 1A supply is the recommended choice. Besides the serial port it has 8 GPIO pins, two of which (IO6 and IO7) support PWM, plus a microSD card socket for FAT32 cards up to 32 GB and a built-in real-time clock that uses a CR1220 battery. The serial port is a 4-pin 2.54 mm header. Check the signal levels in the manufacturer's datasheet before connecting it to a 3.3V board.

Need a different version? See the NX8048P070-011C-Y 7" Intelligent Series HMI LCD With Frame for the framed model, or the smaller NX8048P050-011C 5" HMI LCD. You can also browse the full UART smart TFT LCD category.
It is a 7 inch Nextion Intelligent Series HMI touch display with 800x480 resolution and a capacitive touch panel.
Is the NX8048P070-011C capacitive or resistive touch?
It uses a capacitive touch panel.
How to connect a Nextion display to Arduino?

Connect the display's 4-pin serial header to the board's TX/RX pins, plus power and ground. Power the display from a 5V 1A supply, and check the datasheet for the serial signal levels when using a 3.3V board.
How to program a Nextion display?
Design the pages in the Nextion Editor with drag-and-drop components, load the project onto the display, and then control it from your controller with serial commands.
What serial speed does it support?
It supports baud rates from 2400 to 921600 bps.
Does it have a microSD slot and a real-time clock?
Yes. It has a microSD socket (FAT32, up to 32 GB) and a built-in RTC that runs on a CR1220 battery.
How many GPIO pins does it have?
It has 8 GPIO pins (IO0–IO7), and IO6 and IO7 support PWM.

The NX8048P070-011C Nextion display brings a 7 inch 800x480 screen, capacitive touch, UART control, GPIO, microSD and RTC into one HMI module. Contact us if you need help choosing the right size or version.

name: Raspberry Pi 5 - 16GB

blocks.text: The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB board is the top-memory variant of the latest Raspberry Pi 5 single-board computer, built for power users and professional applications — heavier multitasking, multiple virtual machines, and memory-intensive AI workloads. It's one of RAM Electronics' Raspberry Pi boards, alongside the 4GB and 8GB memory options for lighter workloads and tighter budgets.
Broadcom BCM2712 2.4GHz quad-core 64-bit Arm Cortex-A76 CPU, with cryptography extensions, 512KB per-core L2 caches and a 2MB shared L3 cache
VideoCore VII GPU, supporting OpenGL ES 3.1, Vulkan 1.2
Dual 4Kp60 HDMI® display output with HDR support
microSD card slot, with support for high-speed SDR104 mode
Gigabit Ethernet, with PoE+ support (requires separate PoE+ HAT)
PCIe 2.0 x1 interface for fast peripherals (requires separate M.2 HAT or other adapter)
5V/5A DC power via USB-C, with Power Delivery support
Real-time clock (RTC), powered from external battery
The most memory in the Raspberry Pi 5 lineup — built for professional and power-user applications rather than typical hobby projects.
Handles multiple simultaneous virtual machines, containers, or memory-heavy services without the swapping/slowdown a smaller board would hit.
Pairs well with an M.2 NVMe SSD (via a separate M.2 HAT) for workloads that need both large RAM and fast storage.

Only need extra multitasking headroom without full "professional" specs? The Raspberry Pi 5 8GB covers most everyday and hobby use comfortably. For lighter or budget-focused projects, see the Raspberry Pi 5 4GB.
Common Uses for the Raspberry Pi 5 16GB
Local AI/LLM inference and other memory-intensive edge-AI workloads.
Running several virtual machines or Docker containers at once on a single board.
Professional development workstations and CI/build servers that need headroom beyond typical single-board use.
NVMe-backed NAS or media server builds using the PCIe M.2 HAT for fast storage.
What's the difference between the Raspberry Pi 5 8GB and 16GB?

Both use the same BCM2712 Cortex-A76 CPU and I/O; the 16GB board doubles the RAM again over the 8GB variant, mainly benefiting heavy multitasking, multiple VMs/containers, and memory-intensive workloads rather than raw processing speed.
Is the 16GB model overkill for beginners?
For most learning projects and everyday use, the 4GB or 8GB boards are enough. The 16GB variant is aimed at power users and professional applications that actually need the extra memory headroom.
Do I need an M.2 HAT to use an SSD with this board?
Yes — the board's PCIe 2.0 x1 interface needs a separate M.2 HAT (or similar adapter) to connect an NVMe SSD; it isn't built in.
What power supply does the Raspberry Pi 5 16GB need?
The same as the other Raspberry Pi 5 boards: a 5V/5A USB-C power supply with Power Delivery support, for full performance and USB accessory power.
Does more RAM mean better video/display performance?

Not directly — display output (dual 4Kp60 HDMI, HDR) and GPU performance are the same across all Raspberry Pi 5 memory variants; the extra RAM mainly helps with multitasking and memory-heavy software.

Need the most headroom the Raspberry Pi 5 platform offers? Shop the Raspberry Pi 5 16GB board at RAM Electronics, and pair it with an M.2 HAT and NVMe SSD for a fast, professional-grade single-board setup this study season.

blocks.text: 3D Printer Parts Stepstick TMC2208 Super Quiet Stepper Motor Driver With New Heatsinks Replace Ramps 1.4, 1.5 & 1.6 Reprap Board
Rated Motor Phase Current: 1.4A RMS | 2A Peak
THE KEY FEATURES OF TMC2208 V2.0 STEPPER MOTORS DRIVERS

When looking at the vast array of different stepper motor drivers available to Makers, it’s easy to get confused at which would actually cater to your application best. Fortunately, though, we’ve taken the time to single out the key features that make each of our stepper drivers so great, so that you can more easily identify which drivers you’re eager to use, and which can offer the benefits that matter most to you. So, with that being said, let’s take a closer look at precisely what makes these TMC2208 stepper drivers so amazing.

While many of the stepper motor drivers from the past few years have been quite complex to set up, due to the fact that they weren’t originally designed for 3D Printing, one of the more recent improvements to the industry is in the way we interface with stepper drivers. This is why we’re so eager about the UART Interfacing that these TMC2208 drivers offer, as it allows for far more control than the old Step/Dir method, allowing users to control all of the control lines (EN / DIAG / INDEX / MS1 / MS2 / Analog Current / VRef) via a single line of code.

Additionally, UART Interfacing also allows for quick and easy configuration without having to rewire pins, with the actual software being able to define motor current, Microsteps, Chopper Modes and more – all while sitting at your computer or laptop. Additionally, as if the above wasn’t enough, UART Interfacing also greatly reduces current consumption when the motors are in standby mode, helping to extend the lifespan of the motors and save electricity at the same time.

If you already know what the original StealthChop is, and the awesome benefits that it offers, then you will hopefully be just as excited as we are with the new StealthChop2, which is similar to original, but integrates a current pre-regulator to avoid overcompensation of step prediction, while allowing for more torque during acceleration phases. And while this may sound complicated at first, what it translates to is fewer missed steps or overshot steps, as well as a higher level of power even when motors are caught in an odd rotor position. This means more reliability and more predictability for your motors, and of course the awesome near-silent operations that both StealthChop and SpreadCycle are well-known for.

name: A4988 Stepper Motor Driver

blocks.text: The A4988 Stepper Motor Driver Module is a widely used, high-performance microstepping driver IC designed for controlling bipolar stepper motors. Built on a compact green PCB, this module features built-in translator technology for simple step and direction control, drastically reducing the micro-controller processing power needed to operate motor positioning.

Equipped with adjustable current limiting, over-current protection, thermal shutdown, and five selectable microstep resolutions (down to 1/16-step), it is an essential component for 3D printers (such as RepRap/RAMPS), CNC machines, robotic arms, and precise DIY automation projects.
Simple Step & Direction Control: Enables easy driving with minimal GPIO pins from microcontrollers like Arduino, Raspberry Pi, or STM32.
5 Microstep Resolutions: Supports Full-step, 1/2-step, 1/4-step, 1/8-step, and 1/16-step modes for smooth and accurate motor movement.
Adjustable Current Control: Integrated potentiometer allows precise adjustment of maximum motor output current to protect motor windings.
Intelligent Chopping Control: Automatically selects the correct current decay mode (fast or slow decay).
Built-in Circuit Protection: Includes thermal shutdown, under-voltage lockout (UVLO), and crossover-current protection.
Includes Aluminum Heat Sink: Includes a dedicated adhesive aluminum heat sink for enhanced thermal management during continuous load conditions.
Continuous Current per Phase: 1A (without external active cooling)
Maximum Current per Phase: Up to 2A (with heat sink and forced air cooling)
ENABLE: Logic Low enables output drivers; Logic High disables them.
MS1, MS2, MS3: Microstep resolution selection inputs (pull HIGH/LOW to set step resolution).
RESET: Pull LOW to reset internal translator logic (connect to SLEEP pin for normal operation).
SLEEP: Pull LOW to enter power-saving sleep mode.
STEP: Inputs pulse to advance motor by one step/microstep.
DIR: Sets rotational direction (HIGH = Clockwise / LOW = Counter-Clockwise).
VMOT: Motor power supply (+8V to +35V DC).
GND: Power supply ground (must be common with motor supply).
2B, 2A: Output terminals for Stepper Phase B coils.
1A, 1B: Output terminals for Stepper Phase A coils.
Important Note: Never connect or disconnect a stepper motor while the driver is energized. Doing so can cause permanent damage to the A4988 driver IC.

Is this Arduino CAN Bus shield compatible with cloned Arduino boards sold in Egypt?
Yes, the shield works with Arduino Uno, Mega, Leonardo, and most compatible clone boards, as long as they follow the standard Arduino shield pin layout.
Does this shield support OBD-II out of the box?
Yes. The DB9 connector can be configured for OBD-II via a jumper setting, so no additional hardware modification is needed for basic vehicle diagnostics.
What's the difference between this shield and a standard MCP2515 module?

This shield integrates the MCP2515 controller directly onto an Arduino-compatible form factor with a DB9 connector, micro-SD slot, and Grove ports — a standalone MCP2515 module requires manual wiring and lacks these built-in extras.
Do I need a specific library to use this shield with Arduino?
Yes, you'll need a CAN-BUS library compatible with the MCP2515 controller (such as the standard mcp_can library). Setup instructions are available on the SeeedStudio wiki linked below.

name: WiFi Arduino MEGA2560 With ESP8266

blocks.text: The WiFi Arduino MEGA2560 With ESP8266 is a customized version of the classic Arduino MEGA R3 board, with full integration of the Atmel ATmega2560 microcontroller and the ESP8266 Wi-Fi IC — including 32Mb of flash memory and a CH340G USB-TTL converter on a single board. All components can be set up to work together or independently, and each module has its own pinout headers. The board includes a DIP-switch to connect the modules — for example, USB to ATmega2560, USB to ESP8266, or ATmega2560 to ESP8266 — making it a convenient solution for projects that need both Arduino Mega and WiFi in one place. Via USB, you can update sketches and firmware for both the ATmega2560 and the ESP8266.
Prototyping additional circuits alongside the WiFi module? Our Arduino Shield Working Area for MEGA2560 gives you extra breadboard space designed specifically for this board.
This board pairs the ESP8266 Arduino core with a full ATmega2560 setup:
All of the modules can work together or each separately — each with its own pinout headers
The board has a DIP-switch to connect the modules
Full integration on one board: Mega R3 ATmega2560 and WiFi ESP8266 with 32Mb of memory
Pair this board with our Arduino sensor kit to start building IoT projects that combine WiFi connectivity with real-world sensor data.
Can I use this board with the standard Arduino IDE?
Yes, the ATmega2560 side programs the same way as a standard Arduino Mega, and the ESP8266 side is compatible with the ESP8266 Arduino core, so you can program both from the Arduino IDE.
Where can I find the pinout for the ESP8266 module on this board?
The ESP8266 module follows the standard NodeMCU ESP8266 pinout. Each module (ATmega2560 and ESP8266) has its own dedicated pinout headers on the board.
Do I need to wire the ESP8266 and ATmega2560 together myself?
No — the DIP-switch on the board lets you connect the modules (USB to ATmega2560, USB to ESP8266, or ATmega2560 to ESP8266) without manual wiring.
Is a datasheet available for the ESP8266 module used on this board?
The ESP8266 module follows the standard ESP8266 datasheet specifications. Contact our sales team if you need the specific reference documentation for this board.
What's the difference between this board and a regular Arduino Mega2560?
This board adds a built-in ESP8266 WiFi module with 32Mb of flash memory to a standard Arduino Mega2560 layout, so you get WiFi connectivity without needing a separate module or extra wiring.

name: ARDUINO NANO 33 IoT

blocks.text: The Arduino Nano 33 IoT is a compact Arduino BLE WiFi board built for connected projects — one of the few Nano-sized boards that combines both wireless protocols on a single module. Instead of choosing between a WiFi-only or Bluetooth-only board, this one gives you both, plus a 6-axis motion sensor and a dedicated security chip, all in a form factor small enough to fit into space-limited builds.

At its core is a low-power SAMD21 processor — a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M0+ chip known for a good balance of performance and battery efficiency. Wireless connectivity comes from a u-blox NINA module handling both WiFi and Bluetooth Low Energy, while a separate ATECC608A security chip handles encrypted communication, useful for any project connecting to a cloud service or handling sensitive data. An onboard 6-axis IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope) rounds out the board, making it a practical choice for motion-based projects like pedometers, vibration alerts, or basic robotics orientation sensing — without needing a separate sensor module.

Setting up a WiFi connection on this board follows the standard Arduino WiFi library pattern — connect to an existing network, or configure the board to broadcast its own access point. Beyond local networking, the board can also connect to cloud platforms for remote monitoring and control, including Arduino's own cloud service as well as third-party platforms commonly used in IoT projects. This makes it a practical arduino wifi board choice for projects that need to send sensor data somewhere beyond the local network — home automation dashboards, remote monitoring systems, or simple data-logging projects that report back to a phone or web app.

What sets this board apart from most microcontroller boards is that its wireless chipset can act as both a Bluetooth host and a Bluetooth client — meaning it can either connect out to other Bluetooth devices or accept incoming connections, using the same hardware. That flexibility matters for projects like a Bluetooth-connected wearable that talks to a phone app, or a central hub that pulls data in from several Bluetooth Low Energy sensors at once.
Need longer range instead of short-range WiFi/Bluetooth? The Arduino MKR WAN 1310 uses the same SAMD21 processor but adds LoRaWAN connectivity for long-distance IoT projects.
Microcontroller: SAMD21 Cortex-M0+, 32-bit low-power ARM MCU
Wireless Module: u-blox NINA-W102 (WiFi + Bluetooth Low Energy)
Note: Board ships without a USB cable
What makes this different from other Arduino Nano boards?

It's one of the few Nano-format boards with both WiFi and Bluetooth Low Energy built in on the same module, along with a dedicated security chip and motion sensor — features usually spread across multiple separate boards or add-on modules.
Do I need external hardware to use WiFi and Bluetooth together?
No — both are handled by the onboard u-blox NINA module, so no additional wireless shield or module is required.
What is the ATECC608A chip used for?
It's a secure element dedicated to handling encrypted communication, useful for projects connecting to cloud services where secure authentication matters.
Can this board be used for motion-sensing projects without an extra sensor?
Yes — the built-in 6-axis IMU (LSM6DS3) can handle basic motion sensing tasks like vibration detection or orientation tracking without any additional hardware.
Does the board come with a USB cable?
No, the board ships without a USB cable, so you'll need to supply your own to program it or provide power over USB.

name: Arduino MKR WAN 1310

blocks.text: The Arduino MKR WAN 1310 is built around long-range, low-power connectivity using the LoRa® wireless protocol, making it a practical choice for IoT projects where WiFi or Bluetooth simply can't reach far enough — remote sensor networks, agricultural monitoring, or asset tracking across large outdoor areas. It's an upgraded version of Arduino's earlier MKR WAN 1300 board, keeping the same SAMD21 processor and secure element family while adding a battery charging circuit and onboard flash storage.

Power efficiency is one of this board's strongest points — properly configured, it can run on as little as 104 microamps, which translates to genuinely long battery life for a device that only needs to transmit data occasionally, like a remote sensor checking in every few minutes or hours. It can run on USB power (5V) or independently on a rechargeable battery, giving you flexibility depending on whether your project is stationary or fully portable.

An onboard 2MB flash chip opens up options beyond simple sensor transmission: the board can log data locally and send it later when a connection is available, store configuration files, or hold small scripts — useful for projects in areas with inconsistent network coverage. A dedicated security chip also handles credential and certificate storage, adding a layer of protection for projects transmitting data over a public LoRaWAN network.
Microcontroller: SAMD21 Cortex-M0+, 32-bit low-power ARM MCU
Supported Batteries: Rechargeable Li-Ion or Li-Po, 1024mAh minimum
How is this different from a WiFi or Bluetooth Arduino board?

LoRa communication trades data speed for range — instead of tens of meters like WiFi or Bluetooth, this board can transmit over kilometers, making it suited for projects spread across a wide outdoor area rather than a single building.
Do I need a LoRaWAN gateway to use this board?

For LoRaWAN network connectivity, yes — the board needs to communicate with a gateway that forwards data to a network server. Point-to-point LoRa communication between two boards is also possible without a gateway.
Can this board run entirely on battery power?

Yes, it supports rechargeable Li-Ion or Li-Po batteries (1024mAh minimum) and includes a battery charging circuit, with power consumption low enough (as low as 104µA when properly configured) for extended field deployment.
What is the onboard flash storage used for?
The 2MB flash chip allows local data logging, storing configuration files, or holding data to transmit later when connectivity allows — useful for areas with inconsistent network coverage.
Which frequency should I use for my region?
The board supports 433/868/915 MHz depending on region — check your local LoRaWAN frequency regulations before deployment, as this varies by country.
Need shorter-range WiFi and Bluetooth instead? See our Arduino Nano 33 IoT — built on the same SAMD21 processor family. Browse our full Arduino Boards & Shields collection for more IoT-ready boards.

The Arduino sensor kit 37 in 1 brings together the sensor and control modules most commonly used in microcontroller projects, packed in a single organised case. Instead of buying a relay module here, a flame sensor there and a joystick somewhere else, you get one box that covers temperature, light, sound, motion, magnetism and user input.

Every module in this 37 in 1 sensor kit comes on its own small breakout board with clearly marked pins, so you can wire it to your board with jumper wires and start testing straight away — no soldering required.
It is built for 5V microcontroller boards, which makes it a natural match for the Arduino UNO, Nano and Mega families.
The kit ships with the following modules:
Big Reed Module / Double Color LED Module
Which Boards Does the 37 in 1 Sensor Kit Work With?
The modules in this sensors kit for Arduino are designed around 5V logic, which covers the most widely used Arduino boards:
Arduino UNO — the standard choice for learning and for most tutorials written around this kit
Arduino Nano — same microcontroller in a smaller footprint

Several modules in the kit output an analog signal rather than a simple on/off reading — the photosensitive resistor, the analog hall sensor and the microphone module among them. blocks.text: The CH376S USB Flash Disk Module is a versatile file management chip designed to allow microcontrollers (like Arduino, STM32, or PIC) to read from and write to USB flash drives or SD cards. It handles the heavy lifting of the FAT file system internally, so your MCU doesn't have to.

The CH376S is an upgrade to the popular CH375 chip. It supports USB host mode and USB device mode, and it features a built-in FAT file system management firmware. This means you can use simple serial (UART) or SPI commands to create, delete, read, and write files on a standard U-disk or SD card without needing complex software libraries.

Which Jumper Wire Type Do You Need?

The connector type decides where a jumper wire can plug in. Male to Male wires like this set are for connections between two female sockets, such as breadboard holes or Arduino header sockets. If one end needs to plug onto a male pin instead, choose the PH60 Male to Female Jumper Wires Set. If both ends need to plug onto male pins, choose the PH62 Female to Female Jumper Wires Set.
Can I use these wires with an Arduino?
Yes. Arduino UNO boards have female header sockets, and the male pins on these wires plug straight into them. The other end can go into a breadboard or another female socket.
Can I use them with the Raspberry Pi GPIO pins?

Not directly. The Raspberry Pi GPIO header is made of male pins, so you need a wire with a female end to connect to it. A Male to Female set is the right choice there, with the male end going into the breadboard.
Yes. The wires are joined as a ribbon and pull apart by hand, so you can use them one at a time or keep a few together as a neat bundle.
What is the difference between male to male, male to female and female to female jumper wires?

It comes down to the connector on each end. A male end has a pin that plugs into a socket, and a female end is a socket that plugs onto a pin. Pick the type based on whether the two points you're connecting are sockets, pins, or one of each.

name: Arduino Voice Recognition Module - Speak Recognition, from Geeetech (UART)

blocks.text: The Geeetech Voice Recognition Module enables true voice recognition (not just sound detection)—it can recognize up to 15 distinct voice commands, organized into 3 groups of 5 each. Before operation, you must load (import) one specific group via serial command; only that group's commands will be recognized.
Analog Interface: 3.5 mm mono microphone jack + microphone pin interface
Serial Protocol: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit; default baud rate is 9600 bps, configurable (e.g., 2400, 4800, 19200, 38400)
Common Mode: Returns readable string responses (e.g. "START\n", "Finish one\n")
Compact Mode: Returns concise byte codes (e.g. 0xcc for success, 0xe0 for error)
Recognition Accuracy: Claimed up to 99% in ideal environments
Issue a command like 0xAA 0x11 to start recording group 1. Each of the five commands in that group must be recorded in sequence.
After recording, send a command (e.g. 0xAA 0x21) to import that group so the module can recognize its commands.
The module listens via microphone. When a recorded command is recognized, it sends a corresponding byte over serial (e.g., 0x11, 0x12, etc.), allowing your microcontroller to act accordingly.

The module offers a cost-effective way to add voice-driven control to Arduino projects—like controlling RGB LEDs or motors via voice. However, to maximize reliability, especially in speaker-independent setups, it's key to use a high-quality microphone for consistent recordings.

name: XH-M602 Digital LED Display Battery Charger Control Switch Protection Board Module - For Lithium Battery

blocks.text: XH-M602 Digital Control Battery Lithium Battery Charging Control Module
This module allows for automatic control of the charger while charging 0-120V batteries of any type Li-Po, Li-Fe, Li-Ion, gel, etc.

When the battery voltage falls below the specified level, the module will activate the charger. Once the battery is charged to the desired voltage, the charger will turn off automatically, protecting the battery from overcharging. This remarkably simple device will help maintain the battery's condition for many years. The minimum voltage can be set anywhere from 0.0V to a maximum of 120V. To change the ranges, just hold down the left button for the minimum or the right button for the maximum.

The 220V AC power supply is transformed into 12V DC power through an enclosed transformer, which then powers the main board. One output is sent to the charger via a relay, while the other connects directly to the charger. After setting the terminal voltage, the main board controls one of the charger wires to manage the charger’s on/off operation. For instance, as an example when charging a 48V battery (with a recommended voltage range of 54-58V), the initial voltage should be set to 45V, as this is the point where the four batteries will discharge below 48V during normal use. The cutoff voltage is set at 56V, allowing the detection box to monitor the voltage. When the battery voltage exceeds 56V, the relay will disconnect the charger, removing the need for manual unplugging. This automatic power-off feature not only conserves energy but also extends the lifespan of the charger.

TP4056 USB Type C Charger Module for 18650 and Single-Cell Li-Ion Batteries

This TP4056 USB Type C charger module is built around the TP4056 charging chip and is designed for one Li-ion cell at a time. The input range is 4.5V to 5.5V, which matches a normal USB supply, and the full-charge voltage is 4.2V. As a Type C battery charger module, it can be powered from a modern phone charger or a power bank cable, and the IN+ and IN- pads are available when you want to feed it from a 5V source inside a project.
TP4056 Lithium Battery Charger Module: How the Charge Cycle Works

A TP4056 lithium battery charger module follows the standard Li-ion charging method: a gentle trickle charge when the cell is deeply discharged, a constant-current stage, and then a constant-voltage stage at 4.2V where the current gradually falls. According to the chip's published details, charging ends when the current drops to about one tenth of the set value, and a new cycle starts if the cell voltage falls to about 4.0V while it is still connected. On this board, a red LED shows that charging is in progress and a green LED shows that the battery is full. The chip also reduces the charge current automatically if it gets too hot.
18650 Charger Module With Protection: Using It Safely

As an 18650 charger module with protection, this board adds a protection function to the charging circuit, which makes it a better fit for small portable builds than a bare charger. Even so, a few habits keep your setup safe:
Choose a charge current that suits your cell's capacity and follow the cell maker's recommended rate.
Connect the battery with the correct polarity, because reverse polarity is not allowed.
Make sure the solder joints are solid and use wires suited to the current.
Use a supply within the module's input range, since a higher input voltage can lower the charging current.
Choosing the Right Charger for Your Battery Pack

The TP4056 board charges one cell (1S). If your project uses two or three cells in series, look at the 2S 8.4V 2A 18650 lithium battery charger module or the 3S 12.6V 2A 18650 lithium battery charger module. For packs that need their own protection board, browse our lithium battery BMS protection boards.
How to charge an 18650 with TP4056?

Connect the battery to the module's battery terminals with the correct polarity, then power the module from a USB Type-C cable or a 5V source on the IN+ and IN- pads. The red LED lights while charging and the green LED lights when the battery is full.
What is the charging current of TP4056?
This TP4056 1A charging board is set to 1A by default. The TP4056 chip supports charging currents up to 1A.
Can TP4056 charge more than one cell?
No. It is made for a single Li-ion cell with a 4.2V full-charge voltage. For two or three cells in series, use a 2S or 3S charger module.
What do the red and green LEDs mean on TP4056?
Red means the battery is charging, and green means charging is complete.
What input voltage does the module need?
It needs a 4.5V to 5.5V supply, which matches USB power.
The full-charge voltage is 4.2V, with a charge accuracy of about 1.5%.
It measures about 25 x 19 x 10 mm.

name: SUNKKO® 709A Battery Spot Welding Machine for 18650 Lithium Batteries + Soldering Iron

blocks.text: The SUNKKO 709A is a pulse spot welder built for joining nickel strips onto 18650 lithium battery cells when assembling or repairing battery packs, with a fixed welding head, a mobile welding pen, and a built-in 50W soldering iron in one unit. Instead of soldering directly onto battery terminals — which risks overheating the cell — spot welding joins the nickel strip with brief, controlled pulses of current, and this machine's adjustable pulse and current settings adapt that process to different strip thicknesses and materials.
This machine is a combination of battery spot welding and circuit board soldering, which makes you work more conveniently.
Fixed welding head and mobile spot welding pen are combined together in one machine so that the welding will be more flexible.
Possess the function of 2-18 welding pulses selection, which makes the soldering joint more reliable.
Possess welding current rapid regulator, selecting the current will become quick and efficient.
The anti-static soldering station which controls the temperature accurately,it is suited for welding any integrated circuit or wiring.
The removable footswitches can satisfy the requirement of welding position or sophisticated technology.
The fixed spot-welding head has a pressure-regulating device which makes the solder connections more reliable.
Fixed Welding Head: 0.05-0.3mm(Stainless steel/iron/nickel) Welding Pen: 0.05-0.2mm(stainless steel/iron/nickel)
Why Spot Welding Instead of Soldering Directly Onto Battery Cells?

Lithium-ion cells like the 18650 are sensitive to sustained heat — holding a soldering iron on the terminal too long can damage the cell internally, even if the outside looks fine. A dedicated 18650 battery spot welder avoids that risk: each weld pulse lasts only milliseconds (1–80ms depending on the pulse setting), joining the nickel strip to the terminal before enough heat can transfer into the cell.
2/4/8 pulse selection adjusts how much energy goes into each weld — fewer pulses for thin nickel strips, more pulses for thicker material or a stronger joint.

Fixed welding head and mobile welding pen cover two different working styles: the fixed head for stable, repeatable welds on a bench, and the handheld pen for reaching cells already in a pack or an awkward position.
Rapid current regulator lets the welding current be adjusted quickly between packs that use different nickel strip thicknesses, instead of a fixed, one-size setting.
Removable footswitch frees both hands to hold the nickel strip and cell steady while triggering the weld.
Compatible with common pack layouts. RAM also carries matching 2-cell and 3-cell 18650 cell spacers/holders to arrange cells before welding them into a pack.
A Spot Welder With a Built-In Soldering Iron

Building a battery pack usually needs both spot welding (for the nickel strips between cells) and regular soldering (for wiring leads, connectors, or a BMS board) — this spot welder with soldering iron covers both without a second machine on the bench. The soldering iron side runs independently of the welding function, with its own 150°C–450°C temperature range, ±5°C accuracy, and a 6–8 second heat-up time to 300°C — enough for wiring a battery management system (BMS) or connector onto a finished pack.
What does the 2/4/8 pulse selection do?

It sets how many welding pulses are applied per weld, and for how long (1–10ms for 2 pulses, up to 8–80ms for 8 pulses). Fewer, shorter pulses suit thin nickel strips; more pulses deliver a stronger weld on thicker material.
Can it weld nickel strip onto 18650, 21700, or other cylindrical cells?

Yes — it's designed for the nickel strip and tab thicknesses (0.05mm–0.35mm on the fixed head, 0.05mm–0.2mm on the welding pen) commonly used across 18650, 21700, and similar cylindrical lithium cell packs. RAM's 18650 battery holders (also available in 2-cell, 3-cell, and 4-cell versions) are a simple way to hold cells steady while welding.
Is spot welding safer for lithium batteries than direct soldering?
Generally yes — spot welding applies heat for only milliseconds per pulse, reducing the risk of overheating the cell compared to holding a soldering iron directly on the terminal.
Does this machine include a soldering iron?
Yes — a 50W, temperature-controlled (150°C–450°C) soldering iron is built into the unit, separate from the spot-welding function, for wiring and connector work on the same pack.
Stainless steel, iron, and nickel strip, within the 0.05mm–0.35mm thickness range depending on whether the fixed head or the welding pen is used.
Does it come with a footswitch?
Yes — a removable footswitch is included, letting you trigger the weld hands-free while positioning the nickel strip and cell.

Building or repairing 18650 battery packs? The SUNKKO 709A combines pulse spot welding with a built-in soldering iron in one machine — practical for battery pack assembly, e-bike and power-tool pack repair, or any DIY lithium battery project. Contact RAM Electronics to check availability.

name: DC Voltage Sensor Module (SKU#VS.DC2)

blocks.text: A simple but very useful module that uses a potential divider to reduce any input voltage by a factor of 5.
This allows you to use the analog input of a microcontroller to monitor voltages much higher than it is capable of sensing.
For example, with a 0-5V analog input range, you can measure a voltage up to 25V.
The module also includes convenient screw terminals for easy and secure connection of wires.
This module is based on the principle of resistive voltage divider design and can make the red terminal connector input voltage to 5 times smaller
Arduino analog input voltages up to 5 v, the voltage detection module input voltage not greater than 5Vx5=25V (if using 3.3V systems, input voltage not greater than 3.3Vx5=16.5V).
Arduino AVR chips have 10-bit AD, so this module simulates a resolution of 0.00489V (5V/1023), so the minimum voltage of input voltage detection module is 0.00489Vx5=0.02445V.
Output Interface: “+ ” connected 5/3.3V “-” connected GND “s” connected Arduino AD pins

name: Battery Power Level Indicator (SKU#KA2284)
desc: Battery Indicator Pro Audio level indicator module

blocks.text: The KA2284 Power Level Indicator Module is a versatile module commonly used for monitoring power levels, audio signal levels, or battery voltage levels. Here’s a general guide on how to use it:
5 LED Indicators: Represent different levels (e.g., battery voltage, audio level, or power level).
Signal Input: Analog input for voltage or audio signals.
Adjustable Sensitivity: Through a potentiometer on the module.
Power Supply: Connect the module’s VCC and GND pins to a DC power source (3.5V to 16V).
Signal Input: Connect the IN pin to the voltage source or audio signal you want to monitor.
For battery monitoring: Connect the battery’s positive terminal to IN.
For audio signal: Connect the signal line (e.g., from an audio output) to IN.
Use the onboard potentiometer to adjust the sensitivity or threshold of the LEDs.
Turn clockwise to increase sensitivity (LEDs will light up at lower input levels).
Each LED represents a different level of the input signal.
For example, in battery monitoring, the LEDs indicate increasing voltage levels.
In audio level monitoring, the LEDs indicate the amplitude of the audio signal.
Power the module and provide an input signal.
Observe how the LEDs light up based on the input signal level.
If connected to a battery, higher voltage lights more LEDs.
If connected to an audio source, the LEDs will react to the signal's amplitude in real time.
Battery Indicator: Use to show the charge level of a battery.
Audio Level Indicator: Display audio amplitude in audio equipment or amplifiers.
Power Level Indicator: Monitor voltage levels in circuits or devices.
Connect VCC and GND to a 12V DC power supply.
Connect the positive terminal of the battery to the IN pin.
Adjust the potentiometer so that the LEDs accurately represent the battery levels.
Ensure the input voltage does not exceed the module's maximum rating (14V).
For audio signals, you may need a resistor or capacitor to filter the signal for better accuracy.
Avoid reversing polarity when connecting the power supply or input signal.

Prototyping Arduino, Raspberry Pi, and ESP32 circuits.
Building and testing sensor, LED, and motor-driver circuits.
Learning and teaching electronics in schools and universities.
Testing a design before committing it to a soldered PCB.
Do I need to solder anything to use this breadboard?
No. The BB-01/ MB102 is completely solderless — you push the component or wire leads into the holes to make a connection, and pull them out to change your circuit.
What do the 830 tie points include?
630 points in the central area for components and ICs, plus 200 points on the two side power rails for distributing power (VCC and GND).
What wire size fits the holes?
Standard jumper wires and component leads in the 20–29 AWG range fit best.
Can I connect two breadboards together?
Yes. The edges interlock, so you can snap several boards together to build larger circuits.
What is the difference between the middle rows and the side rails?
In the central area the holes are connected in short vertical columns (for components), while the long side rails are connected horizontally and are used for power and ground.

name: Voltage to Current Signal Converter Module (SKU#VI800)

blocks.text: 0-5V to 0-20mA Voltage to Current Converter Signal Module I/V Analog Output Board

This module is a High-Precision Voltage to Current Signal Converter, designed to bridge the gap between industrial sensors or microcontrollers and PLC/DCS systems. Based on the photo, it features dual multi-turn potentiometers for fine-tuning and a robust terminal block interface.

In industrial automation, signals are often transmitted as current rather than voltage to minimize the effects of wire resistance and electromagnetic interference. This module converts a standard 0–5V (or 0–10V, depending on calibration) voltage input into a linear 0–20mA or 4–20mA current output. It is an essential tool for interfacing Arduino, Raspberry Pi, or ESP32 boards with industrial-grade equipment.
Dual-Potentiometer Calibration: Includes "Zero" and "Span" (Full Scale) 100kΩ multi-turn potentiometers for precise output adjustment.
High Precision: Utilizes the LM358 operational amplifier for low-drift and stable signal processing.
Linear Conversion: Maintains a high degree of linearity across the entire signal range.
Industrial Protection: Reverse polarity protection on the input power ensures the module won't burn out if wired incorrectly.
Active Output: Provides a driven current signal capable of powering remote receivers.
OUT: The current signal output terminal.
Zero Adjustment: Set the input voltage to 0V. Adjust the "Zero" potentiometer (usually the one closer to the input) until the output current is exactly 0mA (or 4mA if using the 4-20mA standard).
Span Adjustment: Set the input voltage to 5V (Full Scale). Adjust the "Full" potentiometer until the output current is 20mA.
Verification: Repeat the process once more to ensure the endpoints are stable, as the adjustments can be slightly interactive.

name: NVIDIA® JETSON NANO 4GB Developer Kit

blocks.text: The NVIDIA Jetson Nano 4GB Developer Kit is a compact edge AI computer that lets you run several neural networks at the same time on a small board. If you are looking for a Jetson Nano developer kit for AI projects such as image classification, object detection or speech processing, this kit gives you a quad-core ARM CPU, a 128-core NVIDIA Maxwell GPU and 4GB of memory in one developer-friendly package.
The power of modern AI is now available for makers, learners, and embedded developers everywhere.

NVIDIA® Jetson Nano™ Developer Kit is a small, powerful computer that lets you run multiple neural networks in parallel for applications like image classification, object detection, segmentation, and speech processing. All in an easy-to-use platform that runs in as little as 5 watts.

It’s simpler than ever to get started! Just insert a microSD card with the system image, boot the developer kit, and begin using the same NVIDIA JetPack SDK used across the entire NVIDIA Jetson™ family of products. JetPack is compatible with NVIDIA’s world-leading AI platform for training and deploying AI software, reducing complexity and effort for developers.
Get started today with the Jetson Nano Developer Kit. We look forward to seeing what you create!
Connectivity: Gigabit Ethernet, M.2 Key E
Others: GPIO, I2C, I2S, SPI, UART
Dimensions: 69 mm x 45 mm, 260-pin edge connector
Jetson Nano Developer Kit for AI: What It Is Built To Do

As a Jetson Nano developer kit for AI, this board is designed to run multiple neural networks in parallel for tasks such as image classification, object detection, segmentation and speech processing. NVIDIA lists the AI performance of the Jetson Nano at 472 GFLOPS, with a 128-core Maxwell GPU and a quad-core ARM Cortex-A57 CPU running up to 1.43 GHz. It uses the NVIDIA JetPack SDK, the same software stack used across the Jetson family, so what you learn on this board carries over to other Jetson modules.
Edge AI Computer With 4GB LPDDR4 Memory

An edge AI computer processes data where it is collected, such as a camera feed on a robot or a small smart device, instead of sending everything to a server. The 4GB 64-bit LPDDR4 memory has a bandwidth of 25.6 GB/s, which helps when several models and video streams run together. NVIDIA lists the power consumption of the Jetson Nano as 5W to 10W, which keeps it practical for battery-powered or space-limited builds. The kit boots from a microSD card (not included), so you flash the system image to a card before the first start.
Ports and I/O for Cameras and Sensors

The kit includes Gigabit Ethernet, HDMI and DisplayPort outputs, four USB 3.0 ports and a USB 2.0 Micro-B port. For hardware projects it also exposes GPIO, I2C, I2S, SPI and UART, so you can connect sensors, motor drivers and other boards. Camera inputs use MIPI CSI-2, and hardware video encoding and decoding support H.264 and H.265 streams.

Not sure the Jetson Nano is the right size for your project? Compare it with lighter edge-AI options such as the Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ 13 TOPS or the Raspberry Pi AI Camera Module, or browse all Raspberry Pi boards.
What is the NVIDIA Jetson Nano 4GB Developer Kit?
It is a small, low-power AI computer for learning and building edge AI projects. It has a 128-core Maxwell GPU, a quad-core Cortex-A57 CPU and 4GB of LPDDR4 memory.
What can you do with Jetson Nano?
You can run neural networks for image classification, object detection, segmentation and speech processing, for example in robots, smart cameras and small embedded devices.
How to set up Jetson Nano?
Flash the system image to a microSD card, insert it into the kit, connect a display, keyboard and power, and boot. The kit uses the NVIDIA JetPack SDK.
Does the Jetson Nano include a microSD card?
No. The microSD card is not included, so you need to prepare your own card.
How much memory does it have?
It has 4GB of 64-bit LPDDR4 memory with a bandwidth of 25.6 GB/s.
Which video formats can it handle?
It supports H.264 and H.265 video encoding and decoding.
Which ports and interfaces does it provide?
Gigabit Ethernet, HDMI, DisplayPort, USB 3.0 and USB 2.0 Micro-B, MIPI CSI-2 camera input, and GPIO, I2C, I2S, SPI and UART.

The NVIDIA Jetson Nano 4GB Developer Kit is a practical way to start with edge AI: a Maxwell GPU, a quad-core CPU, 4GB of memory and the familiar JetPack software in a small board. blocks.text: The ESP32-C3 SuperMini is a compact, powerful IoT module featuring Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 5.0 LE. It offers low power consumption, advanced security with secure boot and Flash encryption, and flexible connectivity options like GPIO, SPI, I2C, and UART. Ideal for smart devices and IoT projects, it supports easy development with ESP-IDF and Arduino IDE.
ESP32C3 SuperMini is an IoT mini development board based on the Espressif ESP32-C3 WiFi/Bluetooth dual-mode chip.
ESP32-C3 is a 32-bit RISC-V CPU, including FPU (Floating Point Unit), which can perform 32-bit single-precision operations and has powerful computing capabilities.
It has excellent radio frequency performance and supports IEEE 802.11 b/g/n WiFi and Bluetooth 5 (LE) protocols.
The board comes with an external antenna to enhance signal strength for wireless applications.
It also has a small and exquisite appearance combined with a single-sided surface mount design.
It is equipped with rich interfaces, with 11 digital I/Os that can be used as PWM pins and 4 analog I/Os that can be used as ADC pins.
It supports four serial interfaces including UART, I2C and SPI.
There is also a small reset button and a bootloader mode button on the board.
ESP32-C3 SuperMini is positioned as a high-performance, low-power, cost-effective IoT mini development board, suitable for low-power IoT applications and wireless wearable applications.

Classic form factor for wearables and small projects
Robust security features: Crypto hardware accelerator supporting AES-128/256, hashing, RSA, HMAC, digital signatures and secure boot
Onboard LED blue light, GPIO8 pin
Why Choose the ESP32-C3 Super Mini?
A genuine RISC-V core (rather than the Xtensa architecture used in most ESP32 boards) — useful for projects specifically targeting RISC-V toolchains.
One of the smallest ESP32-family boards available, at just 22.52×18mm — fits inside enclosures a standard-size dev board never could.
Deep sleep current of only ~43μA makes it a strong fit for coin-cell or small-battery wearable projects where every microamp matters.
Need more GPIO or a bigger dev-board footprint instead? The ESP-32S 30Pin and ESP-32S 38Pin boards trade the tiny size for more pin access.
Common Uses for the ESP32-C3 Super Mini
Wireless wearables and small battery-powered sensors.
Compact smart-home nodes hidden inside light switches, outlets, or small enclosures.
Low-power IoT sensors that spend most of their time in deep sleep, waking briefly to transmit data.
Learning RISC-V embedded development on real, WiFi/Bluetooth-capable hardware.

What's the difference between ESP32-C3 and a standard ESP32 board?

The ESP32-C3 uses a RISC-V single-core CPU instead of the Xtensa dual-core architecture found in boards like the ESP-32S — it trades one CPU core for a smaller size, lower power draw, and RISC-V architecture support, while keeping WiFi and Bluetooth connectivity.
Is the ESP32-C3 Super Mini good for battery-powered projects?
Yes — its deep sleep current of about 43μA is well-suited to coin-cell or small-battery wearables and sensors that spend most of their time asleep and wake briefly to take a reading or send data.
Can I program the ESP32-C3 Super Mini with Arduino IDE?
Yes — it supports both Arduino IDE and ESP-IDF for development, the same as most other ESP32-family boards.
Does the small size limit how many GPIO pins are available?
Somewhat — it offers 11 digital I/O (PWM-capable) and 4 analog I/O (ADC) pins, fewer than larger boards like the ESP-32S 38Pin. For projects needing more pins, a larger board is a better fit.

S1 Button: It is used to switch work mode(default mode 1)
D1~D4:Red LED.Relay work indicator.LED turns ON when the relay working.

LED OFF: It indicates that it is being automatically configured or disconnected from the router when LED keeps OFF.

NC1~NC4: Normal Close. It connects to COM by default status. Hanging when relay working
NO1~NO4: Normal Open. It disconnects to COM by default. Connect to COM when the relay works.
Turn OFF the first relay: A0 01 00 A1
Turn ON the first relay: A0 01 01 A2
Turn OFF the second relay: A0 02 00 A2
Turn ON the second relay: A0 02 01 A3
Turn OFF the third relay: A0 03 00 A3
Turn ON the third relay: A0 03 01 A4
Turn OFF the fourth relay: A0 04 00 A4
Turn ON the fourth relay: A0 04 01 A5
Connect DC 5V power supply at input terminal ‘IN+’ and ‘IN-’ which has marked on PCB.
Install APP ‘EspTouch_Demo’ on Android phone. The user needs to configure WIFI account number and password by MODE 2 at first time to use it.

Install TCP transport tool APP ‘EasyTCP_20’ on Android phone. It is used to send the relay control command, click ‘SWITCH’, and then press the gray square in the interface to input the name and content of the relay control command respectively (the command format is HEX).
Work Mode 1 (Phone carry on WIFI module directly)
It means that the configuration is complete if the green LED flashes cycle from 4 seconds slow down to 2 seconds after power on;
The module sends an AP WIFI hotspot signal, which can be viewed in the WIFI network of the mobile phone, and then selects the network.

Open APP 'EasyTCP_20', click 'CONNECT', and input IP address:192.168.4.1 and port number 8080. And then click 'Connect'.Green LED flashes cycle from 2 seconds to keep ON after the connection is successful. Click on the gray square to send an instruction to control the relay's switch.
Work Mode 2 (Phone and WIFI module carry on router together)

Short press S1 button to switch work mode to MODE 2 when the green LED flashes cycle from 4 seconds slow down to 2 seconds after power on. And then the blue LED turns ON. Green LED flashes cycle from 2 seconds faster to 0.5 seconds. It means that ESP8266 is waiting for the "EspTouch_Demo" APP to configure WIFI account number and password.
Open APP ‘EspTouch_Demo’ and input router password and then click ‘Confirm’.

Wait for the configuration to succeed. When the IP address of the ESP8266 (such as 192.168.0.174) appears on the APP interface. It means that the ESP8266 module is successfully connected to the router, and the account and password are automatically remembered. The next time when user enters mode 2, it will automatically connect (about 20-60 seconds);

Note:’192.168.0.174’ This IP address is dynamically assigned to the ESP8266 module by the router. The address may change after the next re-connection. Users can view the real-time IP address of the ESP8266 module in the device list of the router.

Open the "EasyTCP_20" APP, click "CONNECT", enter the IP address of the ESP8266 module: 192.168.0.174 and port number 8080, and then click "Connect". After the connection is successful, the green flashing from 2 seconds to keep ON. Click on the gray square to send an instruction to control the relay's switch.

The CP2102 USB-to-Serial chip is a more stable, widely-supported alternative to some cheaper CH340-based boards — fewer driver headaches when flashing code.

What's the difference between the CP2102 and CH340 versions of ESP32 boards?

Both are USB-to-serial chips used for programming the board over USB. The CP2102 (used on this board) is generally considered more stable across different operating systems, with more consistent driver support than some CH340-based alternatives.
Can I program this board with Arduino IDE?
Yes — it supports Arduino IDE, along with ESP-IDF, MicroPython, and PlatformIO, so it fits most common ESP32 development workflows.
Does this board support both WiFi and Bluetooth at the same time?

Yes — the ESP32 SoC supports WiFi 802.11 b/g/n and Bluetooth v4.2 BR/EDR + BLE, and both can be used in the same project, though managing both simultaneously does share the chip's processing resources.
Is 4MB of flash memory enough for most ESP32 projects?

For most IoT, home automation, and sensor projects, yes — 4MB is the standard flash size for entry-level ESP32 boards and comfortably fits typical firmware plus some data storage (like web assets for a simple web server).

Why is this board called the "Blue Pill"?

"Blue Pill" is the maker-community nickname for this specific STM32F103C8T6 minimum-system board design, named for its blue PCB color — it's not a separate product, just the common name for this exact board.
Can I program this board over the Micro USB port like an Arduino?
No — the onboard Micro USB is for power and USB communication only. Programming requires the SWD debug interface (with a tool like an ST-Link V2 programmer) or the USART1 serial bootloader.
Can I use the Arduino IDE with this board?
Yes, with the STM32 board support package added to the Arduino IDE — RAM's own STM32F103C8T6 Blue Pill Arduino guide walks through the setup.
What's the difference between this board and an Arduino UNO?

This board uses a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M3 at 72MHz with 64KB flash and 37 I/O pins, versus the UNO's 8-bit ATmega328 at 16MHz with 32KB flash and 20 I/O pins — significantly more processing power and peripherals, at the cost of a steeper learning curve and the need for a separate SWD programmer.

What This Small Solar Panel Can (and Can't) Power
As a small solar panel for DIY projects, this panel suits low-current applications rather than anything power-hungry. At 5V/230mA, it's a good match for:

Trickle-charging a single-cell lithium battery (3.7V) through a charge-controller module such as the TP4056 USB Type-C Lithium Battery Charger Module — never connect a solar panel straight to a lithium battery without a charge controller, since that risks overcharging.
Powering small, low-draw sensors or microcontroller projects directly in good sunlight.
Classroom demonstrations of how light is converted into usable electrical current.
It is not sized for powering motors, lights, or anything beyond a small microcontroller's typical draw — for those, a larger-wattage panel is a better fit.

This epoxy solar panel uses a resin coating over the cells instead of leaving them exposed, which is what gives it its stated weather resistance. That coating is what allows a small panel like this to be used outdoors or in a semi-exposed DIY build without the cells themselves being damaged by moisture — a feature the budget, exposed-cell panels found in some kits don't have.
What can this solar panel power?
At 5V/230mA, it suits low-power applications: trickle-charging a small lithium battery through a charge controller, running a low-draw sensor, or classroom demonstrations of solar power.
Can it charge a lithium battery directly?

Not safely on its own — a solar panel should be connected to a battery through a charge-controller module (such as a TP4056-based board), which regulates the charging current and prevents overcharging.

It uses an epoxy resin encapsulation over the solar cells, which is designed to improve resistance to weather exposure compared to an uncoated panel — though for permanent outdoor installation, a fully sealed/waterproof panel is generally a safer choice.

The epoxy encapsulation supports outdoor or semi-exposed use, but as with most small DIY solar panels, it's best suited to supervised or temporary outdoor setups rather than permanent unattended installation.

name: HX711 Weight Scale Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) 24-bit

blocks.text: HX711 is a precision 24-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC) designed for weight scales (Load Cells) and industrial control applications to interface directly with a bridge sensor.
Differential input voltage: ±40mV (Full-scale differential input voltage is ± 40mV)
Data accuracy: 24-bit (24-bit A / D converter chip.)
Why This Is a 24-Bit ADC (Not a Regular Sensor Board)

The HX711 chip itself is a precision 24-bit ADC with a built-in programmable gain amplifier (32x, 64x, or 128x) and two input channels — it doesn't just read a load cell's signal, it amplifies the tiny voltage difference a load cell produces and converts it straight into a clean digital value. The chip also integrates its own voltage regulator and oscillator, so this module needs very little else around it to work.
Does It Come With a Load Cell?

No — the HX711 is the amplifier/converter board only. It's designed to connect directly to a separate load cell (strain gauge) in a Wheatstone bridge configuration, which is where the actual weight sensing happens. RAM Electronics carries straight-bar load cells in several capacities — 5kg, 20kg, 40kg, 50kg, and 100kg — pick the one matching the maximum weight your project needs to measure.

The HX711 communicates over a simple 2-wire interface (clock + data), which keeps wiring straightforward on an Arduino UNO or similar microcontroller — no complex protocol or extra components needed to read a weight value. This simplicity is why the HX711 is the standard choice behind most DIY digital scale projects built with Arduino.
DIY digital kitchen or postal scales.
Industrial weight/force monitoring on a production line.
Load-detection projects — knowing when an object is present or its weight has changed.
Robotics and automation projects needing simple force feedback.
Does the HX711 need a separate load cell to work?
Yes — the HX711 is the amplifier and analog-to-digital converter only; it needs a separate load cell (strain gauge) connected to it to actually sense weight or force.
Can the HX711 work with an Arduino?
Yes — it communicates over a simple 2-wire (clock + data) interface, which is why it's the standard module used in most Arduino-based digital scale projects.
How accurate is the HX711's measurement?

It's a 24-bit ADC with a programmable gain amplifier (up to 128x), giving it very fine resolution on the small voltage signal a load cell produces — accuracy in an actual build also depends on the load cell used and calibration.
What's the maximum reading rate of the HX711?
Per this module's specification, its refresh rate is 80Hz; the HX711 chip itself supports a selectable 10Hz or 80Hz output rate.
Building a digital scale or force-sensing project? Pair the HX711 24-bit ADC module with one of RAM Electronics' load cells and an Arduino for a complete, accurate weighing setup.

name: HT12D - Decoders

blocks.text: The 2^12 decoders are a series of CMOS LSIs for remote control system applications. They are paired with Holtek's 2^12 series of encoders (refer to the encoder/decoder cross reference table). For proper operation, a pair of encoder/decoder with the same number of addresses and data format should be chosen.

The decoders receive serial addresses and data from a programmed 2^12 series of encoders that are transmitted by a carrier using an RF or an IR transmission medium. They compare the serial input data three times continuously with their local addresses. If no error or unmatched codes are found, the input data codes are decoded and then transferred to the output pins.

The VT pin also goes high to indicate a valid transmission. The 2^12 series of decoders are capable of decoding information that consists of N bits of address and 12N bits of data. Of this series, the HT12D is arranged to provide 8 address bits and 4 data bits, and HT12F is used to decode 12 bits of address information.

name: HT12E - Encoders

blocks.text: The 2^12 encoders are a series of CMOS LSIs for remote control system applications. They are capable of encoding information which consists of N address bits and 12N data bits. Each address/ data input can be set to one of the two logic states.

The programmed addresses/data are transmitted together with the header bits via an RF or an infrared transmission medium upon receipt of a trigger signal. The capability to select a TE trigger on the HT12E or a DATA trigger on the HT12A further enhances the application flexibility of the 2^12 series of encoders. The HT12A additionally provides a 38kHz carrier for infrared systems.

74HC4067 16-Channel Analog Digital Multiplexer Breakout Board

blocks.text: CD74HC4067 16-Channel Analog Digital Multiplexer Breakout Board Module for Arduino
This is a breakout board for the very handy 16-channel Analog/Digital Multiplexer/Demultiplexer CD74HC4067.
This chip is like a rotary switch - it internally routes the common pin (COM in the schematic, SIG on the board)to one of 16 channel pins (CHANxx).
It works with both digital and analog signals (the voltage can't be higher than VCC), and the connections function in either direction.
To control it, connect 4 digital outputs to the chip's address select pins (S0-S3), and send it the binary address of the channel you want (see the datasheet for details).
This allows you to connect up to 16 sensors to your system using only 5 pins!

Since the mux/demux also works with digital signals, you can use it to pipe TTL-level serial data to or from multiple devices. For example, you could use it to connect the TX pins of 16 devices to one RX pin on your microcontroller.

You can then select any one of those 16 devices to listen to. If you want two-way communications, you can add a second board to route your microcontroller's TX line to 16 device's RX lines. By using multiple boards, you can create similar arrangements for I2C, SPI, etc.

The internal switches are bidirectional, support voltages between ground and VCC, have low on-resistance and low off leakage, and to prevent crosstalk, perform break-before-make switching. The board also breaks out the chip's enable pin, which when driven high, will completely disconnect the common pin (all switches off).

desc: High voltage, high-speed power MOSFET & IGBT driver

blocks.text: The IR2184(4)(S) are high voltage, high speed power MOSFET and IGBT drivers with dependent high and low side referenced output channels. Proprietary HVIC and latch immune CMOS technologies enable ruggedized monolithic construction. The logic input is compatible with standard CMOS or LSTTL output, down to 3.3V logic. The output drivers feature a high pulse current buffer stage designed for minimum driver cross-conduction. The floating channel can be used to drive an N-channel power MOSFET or IGBT in the high side configuration which operates up to 600 volts.

name: IR2111
desc: High voltage, high-speed power MOSFET & IGBT driver

blocks.text: The IR2111(S) is a high voltage, high speed power MOSFET and IGBT driver with dependent high and low side referenced output channels designed for halfbridge applications. name: SN75176 - Differential Bus Transceiver

blocks.text: The SN75176B differential bus transceiver is an integrated circuit designed for bidirectional data communication on multipoint bus transmission lines. it is designed for balanced transmission lines and meets ANSI Standards TIA/EIA-422-B and TIA/EIA-485-A and ITU Recommendations V.11 and X.27.

The SN75176B combines a 3-state differential line driver and a differential input line receiver, it operates from a single 5-V power supply. The driver and receiver have active-high and active-low enables, respectively, that can be connected together externally to function as a direction control.

The driver differential outputs and the receiver differential inputs are connected internally to form differential input/output (I/O) bus ports that are designed to offer minimum loading to the bus when the driver is disabled or VCC = 0. These ports feature wide positive and negative common-mode voltage ranges, making the device suitable for party-line applications.

desc: Easy Switcher 3.0A Step Down Voltage Regulator

blocks.text: Easy Switcher 3.0A Step-Down Voltage Regulator - in TO-220 Package.

The LM2576 series of regulators are monolithic integrated circuits ideally suited for easy and convenient design of a step−down switching regulator (buck converter). All circuits of this series are capable of driving a 3.0 A load with excellent line and load regulation. These devices are available in fixed output voltages of 3.3V, 5.0V, 12V, 15V, and an adjustable output version.

These regulators were designed to minimize the number of external components to simplify the power supply design. Standard series of inductors optimized for use with the LM2576 are offered by several different inductor manufacturers.

Since the LM2576 converter is a switch−mode power supply, its efficiency is significantly higher in comparison with popular three−terminal linear regulators, especially with higher input voltages. In many cases, the power dissipated is so low that no heatsink is required or its size could be reduced dramatically.

A standard series of inductors optimized for use with the LM2576 are available from several different manufacturers. This feature greatly simplifies the design of switch−mode power supplies. The LM2576 features include a guaranteed ±4% tolerance on output voltage within specified input voltages and output load conditions, and ±10% on the oscillator frequency (±2% over 0°C to 125°C). External shutdown is included, featuring 80 A (typical) standby current. The output switch includes cycle−by−cycle current limiting, as well as thermal shutdown for full protection under fault conditions.

name: Water Turbidity Sensor Module

blocks.text: The working principle of the turbidity sensor: When light passes through a certain amount of water, the amount of light penetration depends on the amount of dirt in the water. As the amount of dirt increases, the light that penetrates the water sample decreases, and the turbidity sensor measures the amount of light transmitted to calculate the turbidity of the wash water.
The turbidity sensor provides these turbidity measurements to a washing machine or dishwasher controller, with the washing machine and dishwasher controller determining the time of each wash cycle.

These judgments are based on a comparison between the measured value of the purified water (measured at the beginning of the washing cycle) and the measured value of the washed water measured at the end of the washing. By measuring the turbidity of the wash water, the washing machine can only wash the time required to wash the laundry which is not very dirty, thereby saving energy, so that the end-user saves energy.

name: Thermoelectric Cooler 40x40mm - Peltier

blocks.text: Thermoelectric coolers (TEC or Peltier) create a temperature differential on each side. One side gets hot and the other side gets cool. Therefore, they can be used to either warm something up or cool something down, depending on which side you use. The Thermal Tape listed below works very well to attach heat sinks to the hot side.

This Peltier works very well as long as you remove the heat from the hot side. After turning on the device, the hot side will heat quickly, the cold side will cool quickly. If you do not remove the heat from the hot side (with a heat sink or other device), the Peltier will quickly reach stasis and do nothing. We recommend using an old computer CPU heatsink or other blocks of metal to pull heat from the hot side. We were able to use a computer power supply and CPU heatsink to make the cold side so uncomfortable we could not hold our finger to it.

name: PICkit 2 PIC Programmer/Debugger
desc: PICkit 2 programmer is a low-cost programming tool for Microchip PIC microcontrollers.

blocks.text: The PICkit 2 Programmer/Debugger by FARESPCB is a compact, USB-driven development tool designed for rapid programming and in-circuit debugging of Microchip® Flash-based PIC® microcontrollers using the ICSP™ interface. Built on the PIC18F2550 USB microcontroller and featuring dual 24LC512 memory chips, it operates both as a traditional PC-controlled programmer and as a standalone field programmer via Programmer-To-Go (PTG) mode. With an integrated direct USB Type-A connector, status LEDs, and target voltage supply capabilities, it provides an efficient, portable solution for firmware developers, educators, and production line deployment.
Dual Operation Modes: Supports normal PC-controlled software programming/debugging (MPLAB® IDE compatible) and standalone Programmer-To-Go (PTG) mode via the onboard PROG button.

name: IIC/I2C 1602 Serial Character LCD 2x16 Display

blocks.text: This I2C 1602 LCD display shows 2 lines of 16 characters on a blue backlight, using an HD44780-compatible controller with a soldered I2C interface. Instead of wiring 6 or more data pins directly to a microcontroller, this module connects with just two wires (SDA and SCL) — freeing up I/O pins for sensors, buttons, or other modules on the same Arduino, ESP32, or Raspberry Pi project.
How the I2C Interface Simplifies Wiring

A standard HD44780 character LCD normally needs 6 to 11 digital pins to drive it directly, which is often more than a small board like an Arduino UNO can spare alongside other components. The I2C backpack soldered onto this IIC LCD 2x16 module (built around a PCF8574-type chip) reduces that down to just two lines — SDA and SCL — plus power and ground. That leaves far more pins free for sensors, motors, or other displays on the same project.
Default I2C address: typically 0x27 (or 0x3F on some batches) — the same address range used across most PCF8574-based 1602/2004 LCD backpacks.
Changeable address: solder pads (commonly labeled A0/A1/A2) allow the address to be changed, so more than one I2C device can share the same two-wire bus without conflicting.
Onboard contrast control: a small potentiometer on the backpack adjusts character visibility — if the screen looks blank, this is usually the first thing to check.
Backlight control: a jumper on the backpack switches the backlight on or off; removing it lets the backlight be powered or controlled separately.
What Can You Display on a 2x16 Character LCD?

With 2 rows of 16 characters, this I2C LCD for Arduino projects and similar boards is enough to show short status messages, sensor readings, or menu prompts — not graphics, but plenty for most hobby and educational projects:
Sensor readings (temperature, humidity, distance) updated in real time.
Simple menus or status messages for a project with buttons or a rotary encoder.
Clock/date displays when paired with an RTC module.
Debug output during development, without needing the Serial Monitor connected.
Need a small graphical display instead of character-only text? RAM's 0.96" OLED I2C Display Module uses the same two-wire I2C interface but can show simple graphics and icons, not just characters.
What does "I2C" mean on this LCD?

I2C (also written IIC) is a two-wire communication protocol. Instead of wiring many separate data pins to the display, the microcontroller talks to it over just two lines — SDA (data) and SCL (clock) — which this module's soldered-on backpack handles.
What is the default I2C address of this display?
Most PCF8574-based 1602 I2C backpacks default to address 0x27 (some ship as 0x3F). If unsure, a simple I2C scanner sketch (widely available for Arduino) will report the exact address.
How many pins does it need to connect to a microcontroller?
Just four: VCC, GND, SDA, and SCL — compared to 6 or more pins for a standard parallel HD44780 LCD.
Is it compatible with Arduino, ESP32, and Raspberry Pi?
Yes — any board with an I2C-capable interface (SDA/SCL pins) can drive it, including Arduino UNO/Nano/Mega, ESP32/ESP8266 boards, and Raspberry Pi.
Can I change the I2C address if I need to connect more than one device?
Yes — solder pads on the backpack (usually labeled A0/A1/A2) let you change the address so multiple I2C devices, including more than one LCD, can share the same two-wire bus.
Does it need a special library to work?
Yes — libraries such as LiquidCrystal_I2C (Arduino) handle the I2C communication and character display, and are widely available and well documented for this exact type of module.

Adding a status display to an Arduino, ESP32, or Raspberry Pi project without using up half its I/O pins? Shop the I2C 1602 LCD display at RAM Electronics — a practical, well-documented addition to any school or hobby electronics project this term.
